messages.content:
You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 1.8 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 3.6 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.05 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.4 s (cold start: first time output reaches 1.8 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.02 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 1.8 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF nominal).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 3.2 V at nominal: low, so diode drops matter.
  S1: nominal; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: heavy load; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 150 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 100 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 2200 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: weak excitation; Ip = 30 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 1000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: low frequency; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 470 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: Cp +20 %, hot; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 30 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 60 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       2.24    2.25    26.2   0.269      15.2  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S2       1.76    1.77    20.3       -      20.7  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S3       5.68    5.72    84.4  0.0779      14.7  ok       FAIL     FAIL     ok       FAIL    
S4       1.51    1.52    20.8       -      2.27  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    
S5       2.26    2.28    43.5   0.318      10.9  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S6       1.93    1.94    18.8   0.379      11.3  ok       ok       ok       ok       ok      

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each proposal is first SCREENED: with out fixed at 1.8 V, the net power it delivers is
  measured on S2, S4, S6 for its proposed values and a few automatic value presets.
  If the best preset delivers less than 50 % of the load's need (V^2/RL) on any of them,
  the design is reported back with those powers and is not tuned or simulated further.
- Each round, propose exactly 1 design.
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

Round 1 of 24.

This is your first round: choose the structures you think most likely to meet every condition.

Reply with one JSON object only.

reply.reasoning:
*   Goal: Power a load RL (150k - 2.2M Ohm) from a piezo energy harvester.
    *   Piezo: Current source (Ip) || Cp (25 nF) || 20 MOhm.
    *   Conditions:
        *   `vout_min`: vavg >= 1.8 V (S1-S6).
        *   `vout_max`: vmax <= 3.6 V (S1-S6).
        *   `ripple`: vpp <= 0.05 V (S1-S6).
        *   `startup`: tup <= 0.4 s (S1-S6).
        *   `settled`: dv <= 0.02 V (S1-S6).
    *   Issues with FBR (Reference):
        *   S2 (heavy load): vavg < 1.8 V (too much load).
        *   S3 (strong excitation/light load): vmax > 3.6 V (overvoltage) and ripple issues.
        *   S4 (weak excitation): vavg < 1.8 V (insufficient power).
        *   S5 (low freq): settled failure (likely slow stabilization).

    *   The piezo open-circuit voltage is quite low (~3.2 V peak).
    *   FBR (full-bridge rectifier) has 2 diode drops. If V_piezo_peak = 3.2 V, V_out_max = 3.2 - 0.5 = 2.7 V (approximately, for DSCH). However, S3 shows it goes to 5.7 V. Wait, the piezo model is `Ip * sin(2*pi*f*t)` in parallel with `Cp`. The voltage across `Cp` reaches `Ip / (2*pi*f*Cp)`. For S3: $Ip=100\mu A, f=100Hz, Cp=25nF \implies V_{oc} = 100e-6 / (2\pi \cdot 100 \cdot 25e-9) \approx 6.36 V$.
    *   The FBR fails on S2 and S4 (too low voltage) and S3 (too high voltage).
    *   We need a way to:
        1.  Increase efficiency to help S2 and S4.
        2.  Clamp the voltage to prevent exceeding 3.6 V (S3).
        3.  Keep ripple very low (0.05 V).

    *   *SSHI (Synchronized Switch Harvesting on Inductor):* This is a classic way to improve piezo harvesting. It uses an inductor and a switch to invert the voltage on $C_p$ at the peaks, effectively flipping the charge and increasing the extracted power.
    *   *Active Rectification:* Using switches instead of diodes to reduce drops. (The SYNC controller allows this).
    *   *Voltage Clamping:* Using a Zener diode (`DZ33`) to prevent `vout` from exceeding 3.6 V.

    *   *Basic SSHI* (Parallel SSHI):
        *   Inductor $L$ and switch $S$ in parallel with the piezo.
        *   Rectifier (Full bridge or Half bridge) to move charge to $C_{out}$.
    *   *Improved SSHI (Synchronous Rectification):*
        *   Using switches to rectify as well.

    *   Let's try a design that implements a form of SSHI to boost power for S2/S4 and a Zener clamp for S3.
    *   Circuit:
        - Piezo (pzp, pzn)
        - Inductor $L1$ and Switch $S1$ (controlled by $G1$) in parallel with the piezo to invert the charge.
        - Full Bridge Rectifier (DSCH) to charge $C_{out}$.
        - Zener diode `DZ33` from `out` to `0` for clamping.
        - Large $C_{out}$ for ripple control.

    *   Wait, let's refine the SSHI part. A simple parallel SSHI:
        - $L1$ connected from `pzp` to `n1`.
        - $S1$ connected from `n1` to `pzn`.
        - $G1$ closes at the peaks (edges="both").
        - Rectifier: $D1(pzp \to out)$, $D2(pzn \to out)$? No, that's not a full bridge.
        - Full bridge: $D1(pzp, out), D2(pzn, out), D3(0, pzp), D4(0, pzn)$.

    *   *Self-Correction on SSHI:* For $L-C_p$ inversion, we need a switch that shorts the piezo through an inductor.
        - Piezo: pzp, pzn.
        - Switch $S1$: pzp $\to$ L1 $\to$ pzn.
        - Rectifier: The FBR is already present. Let's see if we can optimize the rectification.
        - To avoid 2-diode drops, we could use a synchronous rectifier, but that uses more switches.
        - Let's start with a standard SSHI + FBR + Zener clamp.

    *   Components:
        1.  $D1$ (pzp, out) - DSCH
        2.  $D2$ (pzn, out) - DSCH (Wait, this is wrong. FBR is: pzp->out, pzn->out, 0->pzp, 0->pzn? No.)
        3.  FBR diodes:
            - $D1: pzp \to out$
            - $D2: pzn \to out$
            - $D3: 0 \to pzp$
            - $D4: 0 \to pzn$
            - Actually, that's not a bridge. A bridge is:
                - $D1: pzp \to out$
                - $D2: pzn \to out$
                - $D3: 0 \to pzp$
                - $D4: 0 \to pzn$
                Wait, the standard bridge is:
                Node A, B (Piezo); Node C, D (Load).
                A $\to$ C, B $\to$ C, D $\to$ A, D $\to$ B.
                Here, Load is `out` and `0`.
                $D1: pzp \to out$
                $D2: pzn \to out$
                $D3: 0 \to pzp$
                $D4: 0 \to pzn$
                Let's check: If pzp is +, pzn is -, then $D1$ and $D4$ conduct. If pzp is -, pzn is +, then $D2$ and $D3$ conduct. Yes, this is a full bridge.

    *   *Adding the SSHI part:*
        - $L1$ and $S1$ in parallel with the piezo.
        - $L1: pzp \to n1$
        - $S1: n1 \to pzn$
        - $G1: \text{ton} \approx \pi \sqrt{L \cdot C_p}$

    *   *Adding the Clamp:*
        - $DZ1: 0 \to out$ (model DZ33)

    *   *Adding the Storage:*
        - $C_{out}: out \to 0$

    *   *Parameters:*
        - $C_p = 25\text{nF}$.
        - $L1$: Try $10\text{mH}$. $T_{on} = \pi \sqrt{10\text{mH} \cdot 25\text{nF}} \approx 3.14 \cdot \sqrt{250 \cdot 10^{-12}} \approx 3.14 \cdot 15.8 \mu s \approx 50 \mu s$.
        - $C_{out}$: $2.2\mu\text{F}$ to $10\mu\text{F}$ (S3 needs it to be stable).

    *   Actually, let's reconsider. The FBR had failures in S2 (heavy load) and S4 (weak excitation). SSHI helps by increasing the voltage across the piezo, which increases the current delivered to the rectifier.
    *   The Zener clamp $DZ33$ will protect S3 from exceeding 3.6V.
    *   The large $C_{out}$ will help with ripple.

    *   *Double-checking the SSHI switch timing:*
        - `edges`: "both" (to flip at both peaks).
        - `phase`: 0.0 (at the extrema).
        - `ton`: $3.4 \cdot 10^{-5}$ (start with a reasonable value).

    *   *Component Count:*
        - $D1, D2, D3, D4$ (4)
        - $L1$ (1)
        - $S1$ (1)
        - $G1$ (1)
        - $DZ1$ (1)
        - $C_{out}$ (1)
        - Total: 9 components. (Limit is 16).

    - $D1: pzp \to out$ (DSCH)
    - $D2: pzn \to out$ (DSCH)
    - $D3: 0 \to pzp$ (DSCH)
    - $D4: 0 \to pzn$ (DSCH)
    - $L1: pzp \to n1$
    - $S1: n1 \to pzn$, ctrl: G1
    - $G1: ton=3.4e-5, phase=0, edges=both$
    - $DZ1: 0 \to out$ (DZ33)
    - $C_{out}: out \to 0$

    Wait, I should check the diode nodes again.
    FBR:
    - pzp is the source. pzn is the return.
    - $D1: pzp \to out$
    - $D2: pzn \to out$
    - $D3: 0 \to pzp$
    - $D4: 0 \to pzn$
    If $pzp > pzn$: $pzp \to D1 \to out$ and $0 \to D4 \to pzn$. Current flows through $D1$ and $D4$.
    If $pzn > pzp$: $pzn \to D2 \to out$ and $0 \to D3 \to pzp$. Current flows through $D2$ and $D3$.
    This is correct.

    Let's refine the $L1$ and $ton$.
    $C_p = 25\text{nF}$.
    For $L = 10\text{mH}$, $ton = 50\mu\text{s}$.
    For $L = 2\text{mH}$, $ton = \pi \sqrt{2\text{mH} \cdot 25\text{nF}} = 3.14 \cdot 7.07\mu\text{s} \approx 22\mu\text{s}$.
    Let's use $L = 4.7\text{mH}$ and $ton = 3.4 \cdot 10^{-5}\text{s}$.

    Wait, the Zener $DZ33$ breakdown is 3.3V. If the load needs 1.8V and the max is 3.6V, $DZ33$ is a good safety. But we must ensure it doesn't clamp *too* early, although 3.3V is well above 1.8V.

    One last check: S2 and S4 were the main failures. SSHI is the most potent way to increase power from a piezo.

    Let's re-verify the Full Bridge again.
    Nodes: `pzp`, `pzn`, `out`, `0`.
    Diodes:
    1. pzp $\to$ out
    2. pzn $\to$ out
    3. 0 $\to$ pzp
    4. 0 $\to$ pzn
    Wait, this means $D1$ and $D2$ are both cathodes at `out`. $D3$ and $D4$ are both anodes at `0`.
    Correct.

    Is there any other way to improve S4 (weak excitation)?
    S4: $Ip = 30\mu\text{A}$, $RL = 1\text{M}\Omega$.
    The power is very low. SSHI should help.

    *Potential issue:* If $C_{out}$ is too small, ripple will be too high. If too large, startup `tup` will be too slow. $2.2\mu\text{F}$ was used in FBR. Let's try $4.7\mu\text{F}$.

    *Wait!* The `S` switch $Ron$ is 2 Ohm. The $L$ series resistance is $2 + 5 \cdot (L/1\text{mH})$.
    For $L=4.7\text{mH}$, $R_L = 2 + 5 \cdot 4.7 = 25.5 \Omega$.
    This is very low compared to $RL$, so efficiency should be high.

    Wait, I just noticed the $S$ switch is defined as `nodes [a, b]`.
    $S1: n1 \to pzn$.
    $L1: pzp \to n1$.
    This creates a loop `pzp` $\to$ `n1` $\to$ `pzn` $\to$ `pzp`. Correct.

    One more thing: the `S` switch `ctrl` is the ID of a `SYNC`.
    `S1` has `ctrl`: `G1`.
    `G1` is a `SYNC`.
    This matches the requirements.
